unit.name: System of Particles and Rotational Motion

chapter: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
question_text: a) State and prove the parallel axes theorem. b) For a thin flat circular disk, the radius of gyration about a diameter as axis is k. If the disk is cut along a diameter AB into two equal pieces, find the radius of gyration of each piece about AB.

verification.note: Sri Chaitanya IPE Junior Fastrack (Rev. May 2024), Unit 7 SHORT ANSWER. The mark split is invented and needs a Telangana IPE teacher; no exam appearance years are printed, so appearances[] stays empty. AI physics check 2026-08-24: formulas, signs, numbers and claims verified against NCERT Class-11 conventions; corrections applied to explanation text (why / common_mistakes / memory_tip), marked answer lines unchanged unless factually wrong.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: a) The statement
lines: The moment of inertia of a rigid body
about any axis equals its moment of
inertia about a parallel axis through
the centre of mass, plus Mr² —
steps.margin_note: Say every part: parallel axis, THROUGH THE CENTRE OF MASS, r between the axes.
steps.why: The theorem lets you move a known moment of inertia from the centre of mass to any parallel axis — which is how the rod-about-one-end result in this same unit is obtained.
common_mistakes: Dropping "through the centre of mass" — the theorem is false between two arbitrary parallel axes.

recall.must_convey: That I about any axis = I about the parallel axis through the centre of mass + Mr².
accept: I equals I naught plus M r squared
parallel axis through the centre of mass
reject: sum of moments about two perpendicular axes

steps.memory_tip: The formula is the statement: I = I_G + M d² — the centre-of-mass value plus M times distance squared.

steps.label: The figure
steps.margin_note: Axis AB, the parallel axis CD through the centre of mass C, a particle at P, and PQ perpendicular to the base line. The proof reads off this picture.
steps.why: The whole proof is the expansion of AQ = AC + CQ inside one right triangle — the figure is where that triangle lives.
common_mistakes: Drawing the two axes but not the particle P, leaving the proof with nothing to sum over.

recall.must_convey: That a figure is drawn with axis AB, parallel axis CD through C, particle P and foot Q.
accept: draw the two parallel axes and the particle
figure with A B C D P Q
reject: I equals I naught plus M r squared

steps.memory_tip: Draw the two parallel axes through C and A, one particle P, and the perpendicular foot Q.

steps.label: The proof
lines: For a particle of mass m at P, with
AQ = AC + CQ, the right triangle APQ
Multiplying by m and summing over all
The last sum is zero — C is the centre
steps.margin_note: The mark-winning line is WHY Σm·CQ = 0: distances measured from the centre of mass average to zero.
steps.why: Σm·CQ is the mass-weighted distance from the centre of mass — zero by the very definition of the centre of mass. Every parallel-axes proof turns on this one line.
common_mistakes: Dropping the cross term instead of explaining why it vanishes.
Writing AP² = AC² + CP² and losing the 2·AC·CQ term entirely.

recall.must_convey: That expanding AP² gives a cross term 2·AC·Σm·CQ which vanishes because C is the centre of mass, leaving I = I₀ + Mr².
accept: the cross term is zero because C is the centre of mass
sigma m C Q is zero
reject: each piece has half the mass

steps.memory_tip: Expand (AC + CQ)². The cross term Σm·CQ is zero by the definition of the centre of mass.

steps.label: b) The cut disc
lines: For the whole disc about the diameter,
BOTH the mass and the moment of
steps.margin_note: The surprise IS the answer: both halves shrink together, so k does not change. Say that in words.
steps.why: Radius of gyration is a RATIO. Cutting the disc removes mass and its contribution to I in the same proportion, so the ratio — and k — is untouched.
common_mistakes: Halving only the mass and concluding k′ = k√2.
Calling the half disc a smaller disc of the same shape. It is not; k is unchanged because every remaining particle keeps its own distance from AB, so I and M halve in the same proportion.

recall.must_convey: That mass and moment of inertia both halve, so the radius of gyration stays k.
accept: both halve so k is unchanged

steps.memory_tip: Radius of gyration is a RATIO — cutting the disc scales I and M in the same proportion, so K stays the same.

insider_note: Part b) is a separate mark — the answer (K unchanged) needs its reason stated: cutting scales I and M together.
